title: Continuous Improvement
sequence: runs from the first day to closure. Pull lessons in at the start, capture and apply them while the work proceeds (retrospectives, after-action reviews, in-progress postmortems), and hand them to the organization when a phase or the project ends. Close Project or Phase also forwards suggested improvements to policies and procedures to the owning unit.

toc.title: The Mindset: Lessons Only Count When They Are Used
Help Ensure Continuous Improvement Processes Are Updated (ECO)
Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Term Meaning
Lessons learned Knowledge gained during a project that shows how events were handled, or should be handled in future, to improve future performance
Lessons learned register A project document or repository recording knowledge gained during a project, phase or iteration so it can improve future performance for the team and the organization. Entries have a category and description and may carry impacts, recommendations and proposed actions; it records challenges, problems, realized risks and opportunities. Created early as an output of Manage Project Knowledge; afterward an input and output of many processes
Lessons learned repository The organizational process asset that receives the register's content when a project or phase ends
Lessons learned updates Capturing, documenting and integrating what went well, what did not, and how similar situations could be handled better
Retrospective A regular workshop in which participants explore their work and results to improve process and product; held at least at the end of every iteration; outcomes are actionable, with owners. The word can describe any lessons learned session in any approach
After-action review (AAR) A structured review, usually at the end of a project or after significant milestones, built on four questions: what was supposed to happen, what actually happened, why were there differences, what can we learn. All involved participate; findings are documented and shared
In-progress postmortem A structured review at various stages of the life cycle to analyze current performance, identify issues and implement improvements; periodic, not only at the end
Continuous improvement An ongoing effort to improve processes, products, systems or services by identifying, analyzing and implementing incremental improvements. PMBOK 8 names PDCA, Lean, Total Quality Management, Six Sigma and the Five Focusing Steps as approaches
Process analysis Looks for process improvement opportunities by examining problems, constraints and non-value-added activities
Process improvement A systematic approach to raising a process's efficiency and effectiveness: analyze the current process, find areas to improve, implement changes for better performance, quality and customer satisfaction; the aim is to optimize operations, reduce waste and increase value
Waste Activities that consume resources or time without adding value
Value stream mapping A Lean technique that displays the critical steps in a process and the time taken in each to identify waste; it documents, analyzes and improves the flow from a customer's request to realized value
Benchmarking Comparing actual or planned products, processes and practices with those of comparable organizations to identify good practices, generate improvement ideas and provide a basis for measuring performance
Organizational process assets (OPAs) Plans, processes, policies, procedures, templates, documents and knowledge repositories used by the performing organization, including lessons learned and historical information from earlier projects
OPA updates Any OPA can be updated as a result of a process (plans, processes and knowledge repositories); an output of many processes
Governance feedback loop Periodic reviews, lessons learned and iterative adjustments built into the governance framework so governance practices improve too
Inspect and adapt Reviewing at review points, phase gates and retrospectives, then changing the process, development approach or delivery frequency as needed

2The Mindset: Lessons Only Count When They Are Used

  • PMBOK 8 expects the project team to promote a culture of continuous improvement and reflective practice so lessons are captured, shared and used.
  • Lessons are incorporated during the ongoing processes, not only at the end of the project. This is the governance outcome check for lessons learned and retrospectives.
  • Continuous improvement and waste elimination underpin the Embed Quality principle: teams refine processes, use resources better and deliver to target. Less rework also means a smaller environmental footprint (Topics 02 and 07).
  • A culture of trust and shared ownership matters: empowering the team to find and implement improvements shows trust in its skills and builds pride of ownership (Section 3.4.4). Lessons are about the work, not about blame.

3Utilize Lessons Learned (ECO)

3.1 Where lessons come from

  • Retrospectives (at least each iteration), after-action reviews (end of the project or after significant milestones), in-progress postmortems (periodic), other lessons learned meetings and workshops.
  • Quality audits: they identify good practices and nonconformities, share good practices from similar projects, and record their contribution in the organization's lessons learned repository; correcting the deficiencies they find lowers the cost of quality (Topic 18).
  • Issues, realized risks and opportunities, variances and trends from monitoring (Topics 28 and 30), stakeholder feedback and benchmarking against comparable organizations.
  • Close Project or Phase: final lessons for the project or phase (Topic 35).

3.2 Use lessons at the start and in planning

Use for How lessons help
Approach and tailoring Choose and adapt the life cycle, governance and practices that worked on similar projects (Topic 05)
Estimates Analogous estimating uses actual durations, costs and parameters of earlier similar projects (PMBOK 8), adjusted for known differences
Risk identification Checklists are an effective way to capture lessons from similar completed projects and list risks that occurred before (PMBOK 8); review them and add project-specific items
Reserves and buffers Base them on the specific causes an earlier project suffered (late permits, commissioning problems), not on a generic pad
Templates and structures Reuse proven work breakdowns, templates and role descriptions; PMBOK 8 notes role templates improve as lessons are applied
Stakeholders, procurement, quality Known stakeholder concerns, supplier performance, contract clauses that caused disputes, defect sources and acceptance criteria that worked

Practical steps: search the repository and historical information before planning; talk to people from similar projects; record in the plan which lessons you used.

3.3 Apply lessons while the work proceeds

  • Capture as events happen, while details are fresh; waiting for a single session at the end loses detail and delays use.
  • Act quickly: reorder the backlog, adjust the plan or the risk register, change a working agreement, correct a process. Work performance data also feeds lessons for future work packages.
  • Look for patterns: the same issue in several entries, iterations or teams is a systemic problem (Topic 30): fix it at the system level, not team by team.
  • Close the loop: check whether the change helped (section 4).

3.4 Apply lessons at phase and project end

  • Close the phase formally first (acceptance), then capture its lessons and carry them into the next phase before it starts. A shared sponsor does not remove the closure step.
  • Hold a final session for project-level lessons, even if retrospectives ran every iteration: retrospectives concentrate on the team's process; the final session captures what the organization can reuse.
  • Close Project or Phase also includes: assessing success or failure; managing knowledge sharing and transfer; identifying and documenting lessons learned; archiving project information; transferring the product, service or result; collecting suggestions for improving or updating organizational policies and procedures and forwarding them to the appropriate unit; measuring stakeholder satisfaction.
  • Transfer the register to the lessons learned repository; the final report also summarizes risks and issues met and how they were handled.
  • Early termination: investigate and document why the project ended, record the delivered work and the lessons, then close formally (Topic 35).

3.5 What makes lessons usable

  • Specific and actionable entries: category, description, impact, recommendation, proposed action.
  • Searchable and accessible in a controlled repository, ideally with a way to contact the originators (PMBOK 8 notes that interaction helps people find and use lessons); walk the next team through the key lessons.
  • Analyzed for common issues that can be addressed by changes to procedures; an internal sponsor helps ensure improvements are implemented (PMBOK 8).
  • Owned and checked: someone applies each lesson, and a later review confirms it changed something.

Common failures: logging lessons only at the end · a long unsearchable log nobody reads · a generic buffer instead of using specific lessons · no owner and no follow-up · blame instead of learning.

4Help Ensure Continuous Improvement Processes Are Updated (ECO)

4.1 Improvement is incremental and ongoing

Continuous improvement means identifying, analyzing and implementing small, repeated improvements to processes, products, systems or services. The basic loop (Topic 18's diagram) is plan, do, check, act (PDCA): define the problem and the target, try a change on a small scale, check the result against the target, then standardize it or adjust and repeat.

4.2 Make improvements real

  • Commit to a few improvements from each retrospective or review, put them in the next iteration's backlog or plan with an owner and a date, and check the result at the next review. A long action list or a log does not change anything.
  • Track follow-through: how many committed actions were completed, and did the targeted problem shrink? Beyond PMBOK 8practice
  • Retrospectives alone are not enough for shared problems: several teams reporting the same issue need a cross-team analysis and fix (Topic 30).

4.3 Update the improvement process itself

If retrospectives keep the same format and yield the same ideas, or results have stopped improving, inspect and adapt the improvement process: change the format, bring data, track follow-through, rotate the facilitator, try experiments, add cross-team sessions. More of the same process gives more of the same results, so holding more frequent retrospectives is not the answer.

4.4 Approaches PMBOK 8 names

Approach One-line meaning
PDCA The basic improvement loop described above
Lean Maximize value and eliminate waste; value stream mapping finds waste; Lean scheduling pulls work when there is capacity and limits queues
Total Quality Management (TQM) Beyond PMBOK 8 An organization-wide commitment to quality and customer focus in which everyone owns quality
Six Sigma Beyond PMBOK 8 Data-driven reduction of defects and variation
Five Focusing Steps (theory of constraints) Beyond PMBOK 8 Identify the constraint, exploit it, subordinate everything else to it, elevate it, then repeat for the next constraint
Kaizen Continual incremental improvement; PMBOK 8 lists it among resource-related industry methods (with lean, just-in-time and theory of constraints)

PMBOK 8 only names most of these; the exam asks which fits ("eliminate waste and improve flow" points to Lean; "small repeated cycles" to PDCA).

4.5 Where improvement ideas come from

Retrospectives and reviews · quality audits and process analysis · root cause analysis of defects and recurring issues · variance and trend analysis · benchmarking · stakeholder feedback · lessons learned entries · diagnostics from Table 3-1 (Topic 05): poor quality calls for root cause analysis and process improvement rather than more inspection; long approval delays for authorized decision-makers up to value thresholds; too much work in progress for value stream mapping and Kanban; recurring surprises for root cause exploration of process gaps.

4.6 Organization and governance

  • Project teams own and improve their processes, while organizations provide methodologies and approaches as starting points that support repeatable processes, consistent capability measurement and continuous improvement; process governance should keep tailoring aligned with policy.
  • Governance feedback loops (periodic reviews, lessons learned, iterative adjustments) improve governance practices as well.
  • Communities of practice and subject matter experts can generate insights that improve control processes.
  • Tailoring is not a one-time exercise: review points, phase gates and retrospectives are chances to inspect and adapt the process, approach and delivery frequency (Topic 05).

5Update Organizational Process Assets (ECO)

5.1 What OPAs are and the two categories

OPAs are the plans, processes, policies, procedures, templates, documents and knowledge repositories of the performing organization, including its lessons learned and historical information. They are inputs to many processes. PMBOK 8 groups them in two categories:

Category Who owns and updates it
Policies, processes, procedures (Section 4 calls them processes, documents and templates) Usually set by the PMO or another function outside the project. Generally not updated as part of project work; updated only by following the organization's own update policy. Where encouraged, the team tailors templates, life cycles and checklists for its project
Organizational knowledge repositories Updated throughout the project with project information: lessons learned, financial performance, performance metrics, issues and defects (also completed schedules, risk data and earned value data)

5.2 What to update and where the change comes from

Source of the change OPA affected
Lessons from the project or phase Lessons learned repository
A procedure proven in practice The procedure in the organization's library (via its owner)
Teams with varying checklists or templates; best practices found One standard checklist or template (checklists should be reviewed from time to time, adding new information and archiving obsolete items)
Metrics, estimates, schedules, risk and earned value data Historical information and knowledge repositories
Audit findings, recurring lessons Suggestions for policies and procedures, forwarded to the appropriate unit
A fixed reporting or data requirement that keeps recurring A standard template at the source Beyond PMBOK 8practice

5.3 How to update

  1. Prove it: show results from a pilot or project data.
  2. Document it: draft the new version with the evidence and the reason.
  3. Submit it to the owner of the asset (PMO or process owner).
  4. Review and approve under the organization's update policy.
  5. Publish a new controlled version and retire the old one (one authoritative version in a controlled repository, accessible to those who need it).
  6. Communicate and track: tell the teams, train if needed, check adoption.

Do not: change the master copy on your own · leave the improvement only in the project's lessons log or a personal drive · update before it is proven · let each team keep its own variant when one tested standard would raise quality.

6Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Capture points Phase gates, stage reviews, in-progress postmortems, audits, closure Retrospective at least every iteration, release retrospective, AARs after milestones Both
How improvements are applied Plan updates through change control; process changes at gates Actions go into the next backlog; working agreements change at once Baseline envelope through change control; team practices adapt
Cadence Per phase, stage or milestone Every iteration Mixed
Organizational handoff Final lessons and OPA suggestions at phase or project close Same, plus cross-team retrospectives for shared problems Both
Risk to watch Lessons collected too late to help Routine retrospectives that change nothing Neither level improves

7Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

  • Tailor the depth to size, complexity, regulation and organizational maturity: a small team may run a light retrospective and a shared page; a regulated or large program needs a formal lessons process, audits and formal approval for process changes; distributed teams need an accessible electronic repository.
  • Interactions: knowledge management (Topic 27), quality (Topic 18), tailoring (Topic 05), governance (Topic 12), change control (Topic 29, when an improvement moves a baseline), risk (lessons feed risk identification), stakeholders (feedback), procurement (supplier lessons) and closure (Topic 35).
  • Check results (PMBOK 8): lessons learned and retrospectives are managed throughout the project, and lessons are incorporated during the ongoing processes, not only at the end.
  • Beyond PMBOK 8practice Healthy signs: committed improvement actions get completed; recurring issues decline; teams reuse templates and checklists; new projects cite earlier lessons; time from lesson to OPA update is short.

8Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Capture lessons throughout, not only at the end; details fade and early use is lost.
  2. Use lessons to shape the plan: specific lessons beat a generic buffer; search the repository before planning.
  3. Make lessons accessible: searchable, in a controlled repository, with interaction; walk the next team through the key ones.
  4. Retrospective actions must be implemented: commit to a few and add them to the next backlog; a log is not improvement.
  5. Update the improvement process itself when it stagnates; more frequent retrospectives are more of the same.
  6. Shared problems need a cross-team retrospective or fix; separate retrospectives lack the full picture.
  7. Standardize best practices: consolidate variants into one tested standard (checklist, template) and update the OPA.
  8. A proven procedure goes to the owner of the organization's library through the organization's update process; do not overwrite it yourself and do not leave it in a project log.
  9. Policies and procedures owned elsewhere are changed only through the organization's policy; the team tailors where allowed and forwards suggestions.
  10. Final lessons session at project end even if sprint retrospectives were held; it captures project-level lessons for the organization.
  11. Close the phase formally, then capture its lessons and apply them to the next phase.
  12. A canceled or terminated project still closes formally: document delivered work, reasons and lessons.
  13. Check the effect of an improvement (PDCA) before standardizing it; share it through OPAs.
  14. Regular, short retrospectives are not skipped because things went well or work is heavy.
  15. Do not blame: lessons are about the work; a blame culture stops people sharing.
  16. Do not confuse the lessons learned register (project document) with the lessons learned repository (OPA).

9Exam Q&A

9.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1A team tried a new inspection routine on one production line for a month, and the results meet the target. In the PDCA cycle, what is the next step?

  • ADo: change every line in the plant at once and stop measuring the results
  • BAct: standardize the routine and roll it out, adjusting where needed
  • CPlan again: start the whole improvement cycle over before any rollout
  • DCheck: repeat the one-line trial for another month under the same conditions
Show the answer

Answer: B. In PDCA the change is planned, tried on a small scale, checked against the target and, if it worked, standardized in the Act step; otherwise it is adjusted and repeated. Restarting, rolling out without measurement or repeating the same trial breaks that logic.

S2An approval process takes twelve days, of which nine are spent waiting between steps. Which Lean technique helps find where the waste lies?

  • ABenchmarking, which compares the process with similar organizations' results
  • BValue stream mapping, which shows the steps and the time in each
  • CPareto analysis, which ranks the defects by their frequency of occurrence
  • DControl charts, which show whether the process outputs stay within limits
Show the answer

Answer: B. Value stream mapping displays the critical steps of a process and the time in each, exposing waiting and other waste. Benchmarking compares with others, control charts test stability, and Pareto analysis ranks defect causes.

S3A single packaging machine limits the plant's output, yet management keeps adding capacity to the other stages. Which approach addresses this correctly?

  • AThe five focusing steps: identify the constraint and exploit it
  • BSix Sigma, by reducing variation in every stage equally across the plant
  • CTQM, by asking each worker to be responsible for the quality of the packaging
  • DKaizen, by asking each stage to make unrelated small improvements
Show the answer

Answer: A. The theory of constraints' five focusing steps identify the limiting factor, exploit it, subordinate everything else to it, elevate it and then repeat, so extra capacity elsewhere is pointless. The other approaches do not target the single constraint.

S4At the start of a new project, the project manager wants to identify risks using the experience of earlier, similar projects. Which tool is an effective way to do this?

  • AA Monte Carlo simulation of the earlier projects' schedules
  • BA decision tree of the choices that earlier project managers faced
  • CA checklist built from lessons on completed similar projects
  • DA tornado diagram of the uncertainties from the previous project
Show the answer

Answer: C. Checklists are an effective way to capture lessons from similar completed projects and list the risks that occurred before, reviewed and extended with project-specific items. The other tools analyze decisions, sensitivity or schedule probability and do not capture experience.

S5A hybrid project found that the organization's change-approval policy caused repeated ten-day delays, but the team has no authority over the policy. What should the project manager do?

  • AWait for the end of the project and mention the delays in the final report only
  • BWork around the policy silently and keep the evidence within the project
  • CDocument the evidence and forward a suggestion to the unit that owns the policy
  • DRewrite the policy for the project and apply the revised version to the team
Show the answer

Answer: C. Policies and procedures owned elsewhere change only through the organization's own update policy, so the team tailors where allowed and forwards well-evidenced suggestions to the owning unit. Rewriting, silent workarounds or waiting for the final report neither respect ownership nor help the organization.

S6A team commits to three improvements after every retrospective, yet a year later the project manager cannot say whether they have made any difference. What was missing?

  • ATracking follow-through: whether actions were completed and the targeted problem shrank
  • BMore frequent retrospectives, so that more improvement ideas are generated
  • CA rule that every action must be approved by the PMO before it begins
  • DA longer list of actions per retrospective, so that more problems are addressed
Show the answer

Answer: A. Improvements become real when a few are committed, owned and checked, so progress is tracked through completed actions and the targeted problem shrinking. More ideas, longer lists or an approval gate do not show whether anything changed.

S7Analysis of lessons from several projects suggests changing a company procedure, but nobody owns the proposal and nothing happens. What does PMBOK 8 suggest helps?

  • AA larger lessons learned register with more entries for each project
  • BA mandatory training course on the existing version of the procedure
  • CAnother lessons session to repeat the analysis for the benefit of the managers
  • DAn internal sponsor who ensures that the improvements are implemented
Show the answer

Answer: D. When analysis of lessons points to changes in procedures, an internal sponsor helps ensure the improvements are actually implemented. More analysis, a bigger register or training on the old procedure does not give the proposal an owner.

S8A department wants to know whether its ten-day change-approval cycle is good or poor. Which technique gives a useful reference?

  • ABenchmarking against comparable organizations' good practices and cycle times
  • BA stakeholder power and interest grid for the department's customers
  • CA burnup chart of the changes that the department approved
  • DA control chart of the department's own ten-day cycle times
Show the answer

Answer: A. Benchmarking compares practices and results with those of comparable organizations to identify good practice and provide a basis for measuring performance. A control chart, burnup chart or stakeholder grid looks inward or at something else.

S9A director proposes one large process overhaul every three years, while the agile teams want a steady flow of small changes. Which view reflects continuous improvement?

  • AImprovements chosen by senior managers and imposed on the teams
  • BImprovement only after serious failures, when the need is undeniable
  • CA single large overhaul, since it avoids the disruption of frequent changes
  • DSmall, repeated improvements identified and implemented by those doing the work
Show the answer

Answer: D. Continuous improvement identifies, analyzes and implements incremental improvements on an ongoing basis, and empowering the team to do so shows trust in its skills. One large overhaul, reacting only to failures or imposing changes from above misses the continuous, owned character.

S10A manufacturer wants to cut defects by analyzing process data and reducing variation statistically. Which approach is this?

  • APDCA, a loop for trying a change on a small scale before adopting it
  • BKanban, a visual approach to limiting work in process on a board
  • CLean, a flow-based approach to eliminating waste from the value stream
  • DSix Sigma, a data-driven approach to reducing defects and variation
Show the answer

Answer: D. Six Sigma is the data-driven reduction of defects and variation. Lean focuses on waste and flow, Kanban on visualizing and limiting work in process, and PDCA is the general plan-do-check-act loop.

9.2 Recall Q&As

R1What does the ECO ask under Continuous improvement?

Show the answer

Utilize lessons learned, help ensure continuous improvement processes are updated, and update organizational process assets.

R2What is the lessons learned register, and when is it created?

Show the answer

A project document or repository that records knowledge gained during a project, phase or iteration; it is created early as an output of Manage Project Knowledge and then used and updated by many processes.

R3Where do the lessons go at the end of a project or phase?

Show the answer

They are transferred to the lessons learned repository, an organizational process asset.

R4How often are retrospectives held, and what must come out of them?

Show the answer

Regularly, at minimum at the end of each iteration; the outcomes must be actionable, with specific actions and owners.

R5What are the four after-action review questions?

Show the answer

What was supposed to happen, what actually happened, why were there differences, and what can we learn.

R6How does an in-progress postmortem differ from a traditional one?

Show the answer

It is held periodically at various stages of the life cycle to improve continuously, not only at the end of the project.

R7Which continuous improvement approaches does PMBOK 8 name?

Show the answer

PDCA, Lean, Total Quality Management, Six Sigma and the Five Focusing Steps.

R8What does value stream mapping show?

Show the answer

The critical steps in a process and the time taken in each, to identify waste; it is a Lean technique.

R9What are the two categories of OPAs?

Show the answer

Policies, processes, procedures (and templates and documents), which the organization owns and which change only through its update policy; and organizational knowledge repositories, which are updated throughout the project with project information.

R10Who may change organizational policies and procedures?

Show the answer

They are changed only by following the organization's own update policy, typically through the PMO or other owning function; the team forwards suggestions.

R11What does Close Project or Phase say about improving policies?

Show the answer

Collect suggestions for improving or updating organizational policies and procedures and forward them to the appropriate unit.

R12What should the project manager do when retrospectives produce many actions but few are done?

Show the answer

Have the team commit to a few improvements and put them into the next iteration's backlog or plan with owners.

R13Which outcome check shows lessons learned are managed well?

Show the answer

Lessons learned and retrospectives are managed throughout the project, and lessons are incorporated during ongoing processes, not only at the end.

R14How can lessons learned entries drive organizational improvement?

Show the answer

Analyze them for common issues that can be addressed by changes to project procedures; an internal sponsor helps ensure the improvements are implemented.

10Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
ECO task Continuous improvement (Business Environment Task 6): utilize lessons, update improvement processes, update OPAs
Register vs repository Register = project document (created early, Manage Project Knowledge); repository = OPA that receives it at the end
Capture Continuously: retrospective at least each iteration, AAR after milestones, in-progress postmortems, audits
Use Start: repository, historical data, analogous estimating, risk checklists; during: act at once; end: final lessons, next phase
AAR questions What was supposed to happen, what happened, why different, what can we learn
Improvement Incremental and ongoing; PDCA, Lean, TQM, Six Sigma, Five Focusing Steps; VSM finds waste
Make it real A few actions in the next backlog, with owners; check results; inspect and adapt the process itself
Shared problems Cross-team retrospective and fix
OPA categories Policies, processes, procedures and templates (owner outside the project) · knowledge repositories (updated through the project)
Updating policies Only through the organization's policy; forward suggestions to the appropriate unit
Update path Prove, document, submit to owner, review and approve, publish a controlled version, communicate and track
Standardize Consolidate best practices into one tested standard; update the OPA
Closing Close the phase formally, capture lessons, final session for project-level lessons, archive; terminated projects close too
Outcome check Lessons and retrospectives managed throughout, not only at the end
First-action pattern Capture early, apply at once, commit to a few actions, check results, standardize through the owner, share via the repository
